notes: Injunction dispute over a farm-land lease and a tenant's right to sublet without landlord consent; agricultural tenancy question, not dwelling/room lodging.
Municipal censorship/licensing of moving-picture theaters under the police power; no bearing on lodging or boarding houses.
Slander suit against a telephone company; the fact that plaintiff and a coworker were 'rooming' at another employee's residence is incidental background, not a holding on lodging law.

holding_summary: A widow occupied a company-owned dwelling as a subtenant of her brother, the company's tenant-employee, paying him a share of the rent; the court held that because the jury found the company had consented to her occupancy, she was not a trespasser but a subtenant entitled to the landlord's duty of ordinary care.

quotes.text: If appellee was in the house as a subtenant of her brother with appellant's consent, as, we think, the jury must be held to have found she was, on testimony authorizing it, then she was not, of course, a trespasser as claimed by appellant, and appellant owed her the duty to use ordinary care in equipping and operating its engine.

notes: Occupancy is monthly/indefinite rather than short-term nights/weeks, and the 'letting' at issue is an informal family sub-arrangement within company housing rather than a householder letting rooms to strangers for pay; included as tangential but on-point for the sub-tenancy/incident-of-ownership line of authority.
Landlord's-lien dispute over crops, seed corn, and mules furnished to a farm tenant; agricultural lien law, unrelated to dwelling letting.
Trespass-to-try-title/vendor's-lien dispute over city lots sold on installment; the tenant-cannot-dispute-landlord's-title rule is discussed only as to title, not short-term letting.

Breach-of-promise/seduction suit; defendant's answer describes plaintiff as having 'roomed and boarded' at boarding houses, but this is biographical background about a party, not a holding on lodging doctrine.
Weapons-carrying prosecution turning on whether defendant was on his own rented farm premises; agricultural tenancy context, not dwelling lodging or boarding-house regulation.
Municipal licensing/bonding of jitney (motor bus) operators under the police power; no connection to lodging or boarding houses.
Murder prosecution; a witness's mention of seeing deceased and defendant's wife together in 'a rooming house' is incidental trial evidence, not a lodging-law holding.
Bank-stockholder liability case; the 'incident of ownership' language concerns shareholder liability under banking statutes, unrelated to property letting.

Venue/fraud suit over an exchange of ranch land for city 'rent houses'; weekly-rent figures are used only to value the income property in a fraud claim, with no holding on the legal character of the letting.
Commercial storehouse lease dispute over the landlord's duty to repair a leaky roof; a business-premises tenancy, not a dwelling/lodging arrangement.
Eminent-domain dispute over an additional servitude from an interurban railway on a street abutting a literary society's building; unrelated to lodging.
Election contest over voters' residency/domicile; incidental references to voters rooming or sleeping at a workplace go to voter qualification, not to the legal character of letting dwellings.

Burglary prosecution construing the statutory definition of 'private residence' (a building or room used as a dwelling) for burglary purposes; does not address compensated letting or boarding-house regulation.

holding_summary: Appellant was convicted of keeping a disorderly house on the testimony of a woman who said she came to stay and receive paying men, splitting proceeds with appellant, who at the time had two other women and five men as boarders; the appellate court reversed because the trial court refused to instruct the jury that this witness was an accomplice whose testimony required corroboration, and separately noted the evidence failed to establish whether appellant was actually the lessee or tenant of the house.

quotes.text: she had an understanding with appellant when she went there that she was to stay and receive men for money and divide revenues, and at that time appellant had two other women and five men boarders
There is evidence that she kept a boarding house and had boarders.
We are of opinion the court was in error. Such charge ought to have been given.

notes: Boarding house run as a paid-lodging vice enterprise, prosecuted as a disorderly house; the court also flagged unresolved doubt over whether appellant was even the house's lessee or tenant.
Tenants-in-common partition suit over inherited land and one cotenant's improvements; unrelated to dwelling letting or lodging.
